To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the phosphoproteomes of two human breast cancer cells lines, MCF7 and BT474, are differentially regulated in response to RA.
the RA-responsive and the RA-resistant breast cancer cell lines have a different phosphorylation pattern and a different gene expression pattern.
“RA resistance correlates with the deregulation and the dysregulation of the phospho- and transcriptomes, with consequences on gene transcription”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the phosphoprotein and gene expression profiles that underlie the RA-resistance of BT474 cells.
the identification of the signaling pathways that are altered during the development of RA-resistance in human breast cancer cells.
the elucidation of the mechanisms of RA resistance, a major issue in breast cancer treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the resistance to the antiproleferative effects of RA is associated with the deregulation and the dysregulation of the phospho-proteome with consequences on the expression of a panel of RA-responsive genes.
RA resistance is a complex phenomenon involving the deregulation of multiple pathways, including signaling and transcriptional ones.
the RA resistance is due to the deregulation of both the “phosphoproteome” and the “transcriptome”.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the RA-resistant BT474 cells are not only resistant to the antiprotumorigenic effects of RA but also resistant to the antimitogenic effects of RA, which are due to a deregulation of the signaling pathways that are activated by RA.
the phosphoproteomics and the transcriptomics of the RA-responsive MCF7 cell is different from the RA-resistant BT474 cell.
the phosphoproteomes of RA-responsive and RA-resistant cell lines differ in their basal state and that these differences are enhanced by RA treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a large number of genes and proteins are involved in RA resistance, which might explain why this vitamin A derivative has not yet been approved as a therapeutic agent for cancer treatment.
the RA-resistance of breast cancer cells is not due to a single molecular event but rather to a combination of multiple events that affect the phosphoproteomes and the transcriptional programs.
the RA-resistant breast cancer cell lines have a different phosphoproteome, which might explain the resistance to the antiprogesteronic effects of RA in BT474 cells.
